scope: Three-paragraph existing-reader addition distinguishes order counterbalancing from recovery of a first-encounter question and flags asymmetric knowledge transfer.

sources.author: I. Scott MacKenzie
sources.title: Within-subjects vs. Between-subjects Designs: Which to Use?
claims: Prior condition can affect later performance through practice.
Different condition orders address fixed presentation order, but asymmetric transfer remains a limitation.
limits: Author methods note, not a game experiment.
Does not validate the fictional map/lighting scenario.
Do not adopt non-significant group effect as proof that transfer is absent.
No reading of the cited 1966 paper or copying of diagrams.

sources.author: Raluca Budiu
sources.title: Between-Subjects vs. Within-Subjects Study Design
locations: Between-Subjects, Within-Subjects, or Both?: reading-learning example
Between-Subjects Minimizes the Learning and Transfer Across Conditions
Randomization: Essential for Both Types of Design
claims: A manipulation may change participant knowledge so later exposure is not the same starting state.
Separate-condition assignment avoids study-created cross-condition exposure; recruitment and assignment still matter.
limits: Original methods guidance, not controlled game evidence.
No universal sample size, significance threshold or causal guarantee imported.
Repeated participation remains appropriate when learning/retention is the actual question.

novelty.decision: No standalone reader. Existing memory-reset warning is retained; only AB/BA counterbalancing and directional transfer limitation added.
novelty.search_limits: Public tree-title screening and selected related full texts; not exhaustive full-library semantic proof.

original_scenario.description: Same pump-room exit: A provides a route map, B uses lighting/composition. A participant who learned the route may complete B without using B cues.
limits: No players, measured outcomes, causal effect or confirmed asymmetry.
Possible difference in A-to-B versus B-to-A transfer is hypothetical.
Different rooms/puzzles require separate difficulty/transfer checks; changing decoration is not proof of independence.
